content.audio: Most of us have had the experience of a device breaking just after the warranty runs out, and being told that it would cost almost as much to repair as to replace. It's tempting to see this as a simple story of manufacturers designing things to fail. I want to suggest this afternoon that the reality is rather more complicated, and in some ways more interesting. Let's start with what we actually know. Studies in several countries have found that the average lifespan of household appliances, washing machines for example, has fallen over the past two decades. That much is well documented. What's far less clear is why. Deliberate sabotage is one explanation, but there are others. Products have become lighter and cheaper, and consumers, on the whole, have rewarded that. Many components are now glued rather than screwed together, partly to make devices thinner, which happens to make them much harder to open. Now, my own view, and I should stress that it is a view, is that the biggest obstacle to repair isn't technical at all. It's that the skills, and the small businesses that once did repairs, have largely disappeared. When a town loses its last repair shop, it doesn't come back simply because people want it to. That's why I find the growth of community repair cafes so encouraging. These are volunteer-run events where people bring broken items and learn to fix them alongside someone experienced. Critics argue, fairly enough, that they're far too small to make a real dent in the amount of electronic waste we produce. But I think that rather misses the point. Their real value lies in rebuilding confidence and know-how, which is precisely what's been lost. None of this lets manufacturers off the hook. Making spare parts and manuals available would help enormously. But if we treat repair purely as a question of product design, we'll end up with repairable products and nobody who knows how to repair them.

When Kavya Rao moved into a fifth-floor flat in Bengaluru three years ago, the roof of her building was an empty, dusty space that nobody used. Today it is home to more than forty pots of tomatoes, chillies, spinach and herbs, and it has become the most popular place in the building.

'It started by accident, really,' Kavya explains. 'I had a few plants on my balcony, but they didn't get enough sun. One day I asked the building manager if I could put three or four pots on the roof. He said yes, as long as I kept the area tidy.'

At first, Kavya's neighbours were not very interested. Some of them thought the plants would attract insects, and one family worried that water would leak through the roof into their flat. Kavya listened to their concerns and bought special trays to go under every pot. 'I understood why they were worried,' she says. 'It's their building too.'

Things changed during the first summer, when Kavya had more tomatoes than she could eat. She left a basket of them by the lift with a note saying 'Please help yourself.' The basket was empty by the evening. A week later, an older neighbour, Mr Fernandes, knocked on her door and asked if he could grow some beans.

Now twelve households share the garden. They have a simple timetable for watering, and each family looks after its own pots. Once a month, everyone meets on the roof for a shared meal using vegetables they have grown.

Kavya says the biggest change is not the food but the friendships. 'Before, I only knew people's faces from the lift. Now I know their names, their children, even their favourite recipes.'

She admits that it isn't always easy. Last year, very heavy rain destroyed almost all the plants, and the group had to start again from the beginning. But nobody gave up. 'If anything,' she says, 'it brought us closer together.'

Kavya's advice to anyone who wants to start a similar project is simple: 'Begin small, ask permission, and listen to your neighbours.'

A few years ago, I would have described myself as proudly reachable. My phone was always on, and I took a certain satisfaction in replying to colleagues' messages within minutes, whatever the time. It took a long weekend in the mountains, with no signal whatsoever, to make me realise how exhausted I had become.

I am hardly alone. Surveys in several countries suggest that a large proportion of office workers regularly check emails in the evening, and many say they feel unable to switch off. Some governments and employers have responded with so-called 'right to disconnect' policies, which discourage or even prevent staff from being contacted outside working hours.

On the face of it, this seems an obvious improvement. Yet when I spoke to people about it, the picture was more mixed than I had expected. Tomasz, a project manager who works with teams in three time zones, told me that strict rules would make his job almost impossible. 'My afternoon is someone else's night,' he pointed out. 'If nobody can send a message after six, nothing gets done.' Others valued the flexibility of finishing work late in exchange for collecting their children from school in the afternoon.

What struck me in these conversations was that the problem was rarely the messages themselves. It was the expectation of an immediate reply. Adaeze, a designer, put it neatly: 'I don't mind receiving an email at ten at night. I mind feeling that I have to answer it before I go to bed.'

This suggests that the most effective changes may be cultural rather than legal. Managers, in particular, set the tone. When a team leader sends messages late at night, staff inevitably feel pressure to respond, however often they are told it is not necessary. Simple habits, such as scheduling emails to arrive in the morning or stating clearly when a reply is genuinely urgent, can do more than any official policy.

None of this means that formal rules are pointless. For workers in organisations where long hours are simply expected, a clear policy may provide valuable protection. But rules on their own will not change the habits of people who have come to feel that being constantly available is part of being good at their job. I should know: I was one of them.

Every spring, thousands of volunteers across the country spend an hour in their gardens, parks and balconies counting the birds they see. The results, gathered through a simple online form, are used by researchers to track changes in bird populations over time. It is a striking example of what has come to be known as citizen science: research in which members of the public, rather than professional scientists alone, collect and sometimes analyse data.

The appeal is easy to grasp. No research team, however well funded, could station observers in tens of thousands of locations at once. Volunteers can. Projects of this kind have mapped the spread of invasive plants, recorded the timing of flowering seasons and even helped astronomers classify galaxies from telescope images. In each case, the sheer scale of public involvement has made possible studies that would otherwise have been unthinkable.

Yet professional scientists have not always welcomed such projects with open arms, and their reservations deserve to be taken seriously. The most obvious concern is accuracy. An enthusiastic beginner may confuse similar species, or report a sighting that is more hopeful than real. There is also the question of bias: volunteers tend to live in certain areas and to notice certain things, so the resulting data may say as much about the observers as about the world they observe.

Defenders of citizen science have responded to these criticisms not by dismissing them but by designing around them. Many projects now ask several volunteers to classify the same image, accepting a result only when there is broad agreement. Others use statistical methods to correct for the uneven distribution of observers. Studies comparing volunteer and expert data have often found the differences to be smaller than sceptics predicted, though it would be wrong to claim they are negligible in every case.

What is perhaps less often discussed is what volunteers themselves gain. Interviews with participants suggest that taking part changes how they see their surroundings. A woman in Osaka who had joined a project recording urban insects told researchers that she 'had never really looked' at the plants on her street before. Such shifts in attention are difficult to measure, and they are not the reason most projects are funded. But they may turn out to be among the most lasting benefits.

There is a risk, of course, in romanticising all this. Citizen science is not a substitute for properly funded research, and there are fields in which specialist training simply cannot be replaced by enthusiasm. Nor should volunteers become a source of free labour for institutions unwilling to pay for expertise. The most successful projects tend to be those in which the relationship runs both ways: scientists gain data, and the public gains not only knowledge but a sense that research is something done with them, rather than to them or for them.
